questions.short_title: Advanced airway not linked to traumatic arrest survival
questions.question: A colleague asks whether prehospital advanced airway management improves outcomes in traumatic cardiac arrest. What does this nationwide registry study suggest?
options: No significant association with survival or neurological outcome
It improves neurological outcome but not survival
It clearly improves 30-day survival
It only helps when placed early in the resuscitation
questions.explanation: Thirty-day survival was 1.8% with advanced airway versus 1.4% without, and neurological outcomes were similarly flat, even after correcting for resuscitation-time bias. Event rates were extremely low, so a real effect could hide in the confidence intervals — the authors call the findings hypothesis-generating.

questions.short_title: Untangling trauma terms for first responders
questions.question: According to this review, what keeps the concepts of secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue and PTSD from being clearly separated?
options: Symptomatic overlap and measurement tools built for other professions
They only apply to police and firefighters, not ambulance work
They differ mainly in how quickly symptoms appear after exposure
Each concept has its own validated measurement tool for paramedics
questions.explanation: The review found conceptual overlap sustained by shared symptoms and tools designed for other professional groups, so they're hard to distinguish in first responders. It's a conceptual synthesis with no intervention data, and covered mixed professions.

questions.short_title: Numbers for when on-scene ROSC stops happening
questions.question: In this Japanese Utstein cohort of shockable-rhythm cardiac arrest, what happened to the probability of achieving on-scene ROSC as on-scene resuscitation went from 10 to 20 minutes after EMS contact?
options: It fell from 6.97% to 0.50%
It fell from 50.0% to 20.5%
It stayed steady at around 7%
It rose as more shocks were delivered
questions.explanation: The chance of later ROSC dropped from 6.97% at 10 minutes to 0.50% at 20 minutes. The 50.0% and 20.5% figures are about favourable neurological outcomes, not ROSC probability, and the descriptive design means this can't set transport or cessation rules.

questions.short_title: Sydney COAST registry: trauma shock first year
questions.question: In the Sydney COAST registry, which shock criterion most often qualified patients for inclusion?
options: Hypotension (systolic BP under 100 mmHg)
Shock index greater than one
Receiving a blood transfusion
Needing inotropic support
questions.explanation: Hypotension was the qualifying criterion in 90% of the 257 patients. The other criteria were part of the definition but were far less common, and the authors caution that not all shocked patients were actually bleeding.

questions.short_title: Roadside capillary troponin for chest pain
questions.question: In the VALIDATE study, the prehospital capillary troponin rule-out threshold of <2.2 ng/L identified only 7.1% of patients. What does that figure mean for its usefulness at the roadside?
options: It only covered a small slice of patients, limiting its practical impact
It performed better than the rule-in threshold at confirming NSTEMI
It correctly identified most patients who actually had NSTEMI
It ruled out NSTEMI safely in everyone tested
questions.explanation: The threshold had a perfect negative predictive value, but it applied to only 7.1% of patients, so most chest pain patients still couldn't be ruled out prehospital. The findings also come from a physician-staffed French setting and feasibility was hampered by uninterpretable tests, so it's hypothesis-generating only.

questions.short_title: AR-guided FAST training sped up students
questions.question: After the AR-guided FAST training sequence, which view showed no significant reduction in scan time?
options: The perisplenic view
Morison's pouch view
The pericardial view
The Douglas pouch view
questions.explanation: Time fell significantly in the pericardial, Morison's pouch and perisplenic views, but not the Douglas pouch view. Keep in mind the study had no control group, so the improvements can't be confidently attributed to the AR component alone.

questions.short_title: Fibrinogen concentrate supply grows in Queensland
questions.question: In the Queensland fibrinogen concentrate supply analysis, where did the largest share of supply go?
options: Ambulance services, for prehospital use
Retrieval services
Remote and very remote hospitals
Hospitals, especially major trauma services
questions.explanation: 97.0% of the 24,717 g went to 54 hospitals, with 66.2% of hospital supply going to major trauma services. It's a supply study only, so no link to patient outcomes like bleeding control or mortality was made.

questions.short_title: Paramedic and midwifery students train together
questions.question: What benefit did the peer-led simulation format itself offer, according to student reflections?
options: It created psychological safety that supported reflective learning
It guaranteed improved clinical outcomes in maternity emergencies
It replaced the need for qualified clinical supervision
It eliminated the practical challenges of running joint training
questions.explanation: Students reported that the student-led format fostered psychological safety and reflective learning. Keep in mind this was a reflective practice report with no outcome measures, so the findings are context rather than proof of effect.
